title: JSON.parse happily accepts a string with an unpaired surrogate - and converting it to UTF-8 corrupts or crashes later
assumption: If JSON.parse (or json.loads) accepts a string without error, that string is well-formed Unicode text that any later encoding step will handle safely.

input.display: "\ud800" (a lone UTF-16 high surrogate, with no matching low surrogate)
input.description: A string field corrupted upstream - a truncated emoji or CJK character cut exactly between its two surrogate halves, or data copied out of a UTF-16 source (e.g. a Windows filename or a Java/C# string) that already contained an unpaired surrogate - serialized into a JSON payload via a \u escape.

what_goes_wrong: Both `JSON.parse` and Python's `json.loads` accept the escape `\ud800` and hand back a string containing that single unpaired surrogate, with no error. The corruption surfaces later and differently in each language: encoding that Python string to UTF-8 raises `UnicodeEncodeError`, while in Node, `Buffer.from(s, "utf8")` silently replaces the lone surrogate with the U+FFFD replacement character - no exception, no warning, just a quietly different byte sequence than the one sent.
why: JSON strings are defined over Unicode code points via `\uXXXX` escapes, and RFC 8259 section 8.2 explicitly notes that the grammar allows an escape for a lone surrogate, leaving the behaviour of receiving software unpredictable - a parser that checks syntax is not required to check that the resulting text is well-formed Unicode. JavaScript strings are UTF-16 code unit sequences and can hold an unpaired surrogate without complaint, so `JSON.parse`/`JSON.stringify` round-trip it fine as a JS value. Python `str` objects are sequences of Unicode code points (including surrogates, which Python represents but which are not valid scalar values), so `json.loads` accepts the escape too - the failure only appears once something tries to encode that code point as actual UTF-8 bytes, because UTF-8 has no legal encoding for a surrogate on its own.

repros.code:
import json
s = json.loads('"\\ud800"')
print(len(s), hex(ord(s)))
try:
    s.encode("utf-8")
except UnicodeEncodeError as e:
    print("UnicodeEncodeError:", e)
repros.expected_output:
1 0xd800
UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\ud800' in position 0: surrogates not allowed

fix: Check that decoded JSON strings are well-formed Unicode before re-encoding them: in Python, `s.encode("utf-8")` (strict) raises on a lone surrogate; in JavaScript, `s.isWellFormed()` (Node 20+, ES2024) returns false for it, and `s.toWellFormed()` substitutes U+FFFD explicitly. Do this before `Buffer.from(s, "utf8")`, which substitutes silently.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #15 glossary: Unpaired Surrogate

test_cases.note: their_parse_json(text) may legitimately accept this string, but whatever encodes the result to UTF-8 downstream must handle (reject or substitute) an unpaired surrogate rather than silently corrupting it.
